result: The authors established stable transgenic pig lines co-expressing NSP-degrading enzymes (β-glucanase and xylanase) and phytase in saliva by selecting optimal enzyme candidates based on activity, stability, and resistance to digestive enzymes, then constructing a polycistronic transgene cassette.
evaluation: Claims C28-C45 collectively demonstrate successful selection of optimal enzyme candidates (C29-C43) based on systematic characterization of activity, pH stability, and protease resistance, followed by construction and validation of a functional fusion construct (C44-C45). The data from multiple figures support enzyme selection and expression, though C46 notes reduced activity in the fusion construct.

result: Transgenic pigs were generated via somatic cell nuclear transfer, producing 33 live piglets of which 25 were transgene-positive, with 19 carrying single-copy integrations at defined genomic loci (Legumain intron 1 or CEP112 intron 5), and 16 piglets surviving to weaning.
evaluation: Claims C47-C62 provide comprehensive documentation of transgenic pig generation with molecular characterization via PCR, Southern blotting, and sequencing (C54-C59). The data demonstrate successful SCNT with defined integration sites, though survival rates were modest with only 16/33 piglets reaching weaning (C60).

result: The transgenes were specifically expressed in salivary glands (parotid, submandibular, sublingual) with no ectopic expression detected, producing functional β-glucanase (0.3-2.3 U/mg), xylanase (0.6-2.4 U/mg), and phytase (0.5-5.7 U/mg) in saliva.
evaluation: Claims C63-C70 demonstrate tissue-specific transgene expression via RT-PCR (C63-C65), Western blot (C67), and enzymatic assays (C68-C70) with supporting data in Figures 2A-E. The absence of ectopic expression (C66) and quantitative enzyme activities provide strong evidence for functional salivary gland-specific expression.

result: Transgenic line 2 pigs were successfully bred through F1 and F2 generations with Mendelian inheritance, producing enzymes at levels of 920-2,935 U/kg diet in grower and finisher pigs, with saliva secretion and enzyme activity primarily occurring during feeding time.
evaluation: Claims C71-C85 document successful breeding (C71-C72), quantitative enzyme production (C73-C78) supported by Table 1, and temporal patterns of saliva secretion (C79-C85) supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2. The data demonstrate stable transgene transmission and functional enzyme production, though C80 offers speculation about lower finisher pig saliva volume.

result: Transgenic pigs fed corn-soybean (CS) or wheat-corn-soybean-bran (WCSB) diets showed significantly increased apparent total tract digestibility of dry matter, phosphorus, nitrogen, and calcium, with fecal N and P excretion reduced by 23.2-45.8% compared to wild-type littermates.
evaluation: Claims C86-C92 present digestibility and nutrient excretion data supported by Figure 3A-B with appropriate statistical analysis (ANCOVA). The improvements in nutrient digestibility and reductions in fecal output are well-documented across both diet types, providing strong evidence for enhanced feed utilization.

result: Serum biochemical analysis of transgenic pigs showed lower alkaline phosphatase activity, higher phosphorus and glucose levels, and slightly elevated D-xylose compared to wild-type littermates, with no differences in calcium, zinc, urea nitrogen, uric acid, or total protein.
evaluation: Claims C93-C97 report serum biochemical endpoints supported by Table 2 with statistical comparisons. The pattern of changes (lower alkaline phosphatase, higher P and glucose) is consistent with improved nutrient utilization, though the biological significance of some changes requires interpretation.

result: Transgenic pigs exhibited superior growth performance compared to wild-type littermates, with 23.0-24.4% higher average daily gain, 11.5-14.5% improved feed conversion rate, and 19.2-21.9% reduction in time to reach market weight (115 kg), across both boars and gilts.
evaluation: Claims C98-C111 present comprehensive growth performance data supported by Figure 4 and Supplementary file 6, with appropriate statistical analysis showing significant improvements in ADG, FCR, and days to market. The consistency across sexes and multiple metrics provides strong evidence for enhanced growth performance.

result: The multi-transgenic pigs demonstrated phosphorus retention rates of 54.7-67.3% and total P output reductions of 21.3-44.2%, with performance comparable to previously reported high-expression phytase transgenic pigs despite lower enzyme expression levels, and enzyme production levels exceeding typical dietary supplements.
evaluation: Claims C112-C127 compare the current results with prior transgenic pig studies (C125-C126) and dietary supplementation approaches. The data show effective P reduction despite lower expression than previous models, though C127 offers speculation about causes of differences. The comparison is well-supported by citations and experimental data.

result: Nitrogen digestibility was significantly enhanced in transgenic pigs across all diets tested, with 24.0% reduction in fecal N excretion in grower pigs, attributed to synergistic effects of NSP-degrading enzymes and phytase in degrading cell wall polysaccharides and releasing encapsulated nutrients.
evaluation: Claims C128-C143 present nitrogen digestibility improvements with mechanistic interpretation supported by prior literature (C133, C135-C136, C142). The proposed mechanism (C131-C132, C139-C140, C143) is reasonable but represents inference rather than direct demonstration. The N reduction data (C141) is well-supported.

result: Transgenic pigs displayed better growth performance than conventional pigs fed diets without supplemental phosphorus, with faster body weight gain, greater feed efficiency, and serum biochemical indicators (enhanced P, glucose, xylose; decreased alkaline phosphatase) signifying improved nutrient utilization and bone development.
evaluation: Claims C144-C149 summarize growth and physiological improvements with supporting data from earlier claims. C148 and C149 provide interpretation of serum measurements, with C149 supported by citations. The integration of growth performance and biochemical indicators provides coherent evidence for improved nutrient utilization.

result: Cloned piglets showed high mortality rates with 30.3% dying from malformation and 18.2% from weakness, consistent with previous reports of cloned pig mortality, with high death rates observed in both transgenic and non-transgenic cloned pigs suggesting the mortality relates to cloning technique rather than transgene effects.
evaluation: Claims C154-C160 document mortality rates (C154) with comparison to prior studies (C156-C158) and inference about causation (C160) based on similar mortality in non-transgenic clones (C159). While C155 offers speculation about causes, the overall pattern supports a cloning-related rather than transgene-related mortality issue.

result: Transgene integration occurred in introns of Legumain (line 1) and CEP112 (line 2), with no significant phenotypic differences observed between transgenic and wild-type pigs, suggesting minimal disruption of host gene function despite integration into coding genes.
evaluation: Claims C161-C169 characterize integration sites (C161) with background on disrupted genes (C162-C167) and assessment of phenotypic impact (C168-C169). The inference that intronic integration minimizes disruption (C168) is reasonable, and the observation of no phenotypic differences (C169) supports this, though longer-term or more detailed phenotyping might reveal subtle effects.

result: The transgenic pigs exhibited significantly enhanced digestibility of feed nitrogen, phosphorus, calcium, and other minerals, produced manure with 23.2-45.8% reduced N and P emissions, showed 23.0-24.4% improved growth rate and 11.5-14.5% better feed conversion, representing a valuable biological solution for improving feed efficiency and reducing environmental impact in livestock production.
evaluation: Claims C150-C174 provide summary statements of the major findings, integrating digestibility improvements (C150), emission reductions (C151, C170), and growth enhancements (C152, C171-C173). These conclusions are well-supported by the experimental data presented throughout the study, though C153 and C174 represent broader interpretive claims about agricultural applications.

result: The introduction establishes the agricultural and environmental context for the study, documenting global pig production, inefficient nitrogen and phosphorus utilization in conventional pig diets, environmental pollution from livestock waste, the role of NSPs and phytates as anti-nutritional factors, and prior approaches including dietary enzyme supplementation and previous transgenic phytase pigs.
evaluation: Claims C1-C27 provide background information supported by appropriate citations to establish the rationale for the study. These claims document established knowledge about pig production (C1-C12), feed composition and anti-nutritional factors (C13-C21), and prior mitigation strategies (C22-C27). The knowledge gap (C27) motivates the current work.
